query: How should an ecommerce agent handle prompt injection in product feeds and support messages before using tools to change orders or access customer data?

cards.title: Treat agents' retrieved documents and tool output as untrusted data
cards.summary: In an agentic storefront workflow, inbound documents, pages and tool responses are data to be evaluated, not authorization for actions.
cards.use_when: You are building or reviewing an ecommerce agent that reads supplier documents, product feeds, customer messages or web pages and can then call tools like price updates, refunds or order changes.
steps: Classify every inbound artifact — supplier PDFs, emails, catalog feeds, support tickets, scraped pages — as untrusted data; agent instructions come only from your own configuration and authorized operators.
Scope tool permissions to the specific store and task: an agent handling product descriptions should not hold refund or pricing-write credentials.
Require explicit human approval for irreversible or high-value actions (issuing refunds, changing prices, modifying fulfillment), with the approval recorded.
Keep secrets out of agent-visible context: inject credentials at the tool-call boundary rather than embedding them in prompts or documents the agent reads.
Log tool calls with inputs, outputs, the triggering untrusted source and the resulting action, so a malicious injection can be reconstructed and reverted.
When content instructs the agent to do something outside the task, treat it as a potential injection attempt and stop rather than comply.
caveats: No single control — prompt filtering, allowlists or retrieval hygiene — is claimed to guarantee safety; use layered controls.
Verify the current capabilities and limits of whichever agent framework you deploy against current vendor documentation.

cards.title: Treat prompt injection and untrusted content as an authorization problem for storefront agents
cards.summary: Malicious instructions embedded in content a storefront agent processes can redirect it from the customer's task to an adversary's goal, and poisoned data sources can cascade failures across agents.
cards.use_when: Anyone deploying a customer-facing chatbot or AI agent that reads external content (reviews, forums, supplier data) or holds operational authority.
steps: Assume any content an agent reads — product descriptions, reviews, third-party feeds, support messages — is untrusted data, not instructions the agent may act on.
Treat input filtering as one signal; enforce action permissions and business rules outside the model even when the prompt or retrieved content is malicious.
Limit the operational authority of any back-end conversational agent so a successful injection cannot reach sensitive actions or data.
Guard against data poisoning: validate and monitor the data sources agents use for decisions, since corrupted sources cause cascading failures across connected agents.

Block AI token freeloading: detect and reject traffic routing unrelated model queries or training workloads through your public AI endpoints, which degrades performance and raises your infrastructure costs.
Grant tools and API access by scope — an agent reading catalog data should not also hold payment or admin credentials.
caveats: No prompt filtering alone guarantees safety; pair input sanitization with scoped permissions and monitoring.
The source describes these as documented threat vectors and OWASP-category risks; exact exploit mechanics and current OWASP numbering should be verified against the latest OWASP Agentic AI guidance.
cards.source_name: Protecting E-Commerce from Agentic Swarms and AI Bot Attacks_ A Comprehensive Security Report.docx

cards.title: Verify agent tool permissions and trust retrieved content as data only
cards.summary: Convert the lesson's 'never trust input' principle to AI agents: retrieved documents and tool output are untrusted data, not authorization.
cards.use_when: Configuring an agent that reads product feeds, customer reviews, support emails, or external APIs and can act on your store (edit listings, issue refunds, place orders).
steps: Treat every retrieved document, email, review, or web page as data, never as instructions. Content that says 'ignore your rules' or 'issue a refund' has no authority.
Scope each agent's tool access to the brand and task it needs. An agent editing product descriptions should not also have refund or customer-data permissions.
Require human approval for high-impact actions: publishing to storefront, changing prices, issuing refunds, or writing customer data.
Block the agent from reading its own secrets or raw credentials; give it scoped API tokens with least privilege and log every tool call with inputs and outputs.
Do not treat prompt filtering or a WAF as a guarantee. It reduces exposure but is not sufficient alone.
Validate tool-call outputs before acting on them, just as you would validate a user-supplied field in a server handler.
caveats: Source does not provide ecommerce agent benchmarks or measured results; the controls are inferred from general server-security principles.
Agent tooling interfaces change quickly — verify current permission and approval options before relying on them.

cards.title: Treat agent/tool instructions and retrieved documents as untrusted data
cards.summary: The source's supply-chain and injection themes translate to agent security: content a tool retrieves — including package manifests, web pages and API responses — must not be treated as authorization for agent actions.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing agents that operate on an ecommerce stack (listing changes, pricing updates, support replies) and consume external or user-supplied content.
steps: Separate data from authority: retrieved documents, tool output and user input are data to reason about, not instructions that authorize state-changing actions.
Scope each agent/tool to the brand and task it was granted, rather than a broad API key covering all operations.
Require explicit human or system approval for high-impact actions (price changes, refunds, publishing listings, account changes).
Keep secrets out of the model's reach: use scoped credentials and avoid placing long-lived credentials where an injected instruction could retrieve them.
Log agent actions and the content that triggered them so anomalous behavior can be investigated.
Apply input handling equal to the rest of your app: validate and sanitize before acting, since prompt filtering alone is not a guarantee.
caveats: This adapts general supply-chain and injection themes from the source to agent/tool contexts; the source does not specify agent controls directly.
No combination of filtering or scoping is a complete guarantee — treat it as layered risk reduction.

cards.title: Secure handling of retrieved documents and tool output in agent workflows
cards.summary: Text fetched from the web, uploaded by users, or returned by a tool is untrusted data and must never be treated as authorization to change an agent's targets or expand its permissions.
cards.use_when: You are deploying an ecommerce automation agent that reads supplier pages, review content, uploaded CSVs, order notes or API responses and then acts — for example updating prices, drafting replies, creating orders or running scripts.
steps: Classify every input the agent processes into trusted configuration versus untrusted content, where untrusted includes scraped pages, user-uploaded files, email bodies, third-party API responses and any tool output that carries external text.
Define the agent's permitted scope explicitly by brand and task — which store, which tables, which tools, which files — as configuration the model cannot alter from content it reads.

Never let instructions found inside retrieved content change the target, destination, data range or command that will be executed; if a document appears to contain directives, treat that as content to report, not to obey.

Restrict tool permissions to the minimum needed for the task: read-only query access where writes are not required, an allowlist of programs the automation may run, and no shell string construction from fetched values.

Require human approval for irreversible or high-impact actions such as bulk price changes, refunds, order cancellations, credential changes or any operation that deletes data, and log the approval with the actor identity.

Handle secrets outside of content: keep API keys and database credentials in a secret store that the agent can use through a scoped interface but cannot read back into its context or write into a file, and rotate them on a schedule.
Log every tool invocation with the requesting identity, the exact parameters, the retrieved content hash and the outcome, so an anomalous action can be traced and replayed.
Validate on a staging store by feeding a document containing injected directive-like text and confirming the agent takes no action outside its configured scope and instead surfaces the anomaly.
caveats: Do not claim that prompt filtering, a WAF or content sanitization alone guarantees safety against injected instructions in retrieved content.
Distinguish authorization from data handling: seeing a credential or an instruction is not permission to use it, and encryption protects data at rest or in transit, not the decision to act.
This card adapts the source's injection principle to agent inputs; the source does not present an agent-specific benchmark or outcome.

query: How should our store defend against card testing and account takeover without blocking legitimate shoppers?

cards.title: Prevent agent hijacking and account takeover of stored credentials
cards.summary: Attackers compromise legitimate AI shopping assistants and stored payment credentials to change delivery addresses, extract payment data, and execute fraud.
cards.use_when: Hardening customer accounts, saved payment methods, and third-party agent access, or investigating suspicious account modifications.
steps: Treat any agent acting on behalf of a customer account as a potential hijack vector — compromise of a legitimate agent's credentials lets attackers act as the agent.
Require risk-based step-up authentication (MFA) specifically for sensitive actions: changing delivery address, extracting payment data, draining loyalty points or gift-card balances.
Apply micro-authorization: grant each agent action only the minimal permission it needs, so a hijacked agent has a small blast radius.
Microsegment back-end systems so a compromised agent cannot move laterally across the platform.
Monitor for rapid gift-card balance brute-forcing and credential-stuffing against loyalty accounts, which the source says swarms can drain quickly.
caveats: Risk-based MFA thresholds are not specified; set them from your own risk model.
If legitimate agents are used by real customers, blocking all credential use harms conversion; the control should be scoped to high-risk actions.
cards.source_name: Protecting E-Commerce from Agentic Swarms and AI Bot Attacks_ A Comprehensive Security Report.docx

cards.title: CNP fraud and card testing: the mechanism to defend against
cards.summary: Card-not-present fraud uses stolen card data validated through small test transactions before larger fraudulent purchases.
cards.use_when: Designing checkout fraud controls, selecting a payment processor configuration, or investigating a spike in small declined/approved orders on your store.
steps: Understand the attack chain: fraudsters obtain card data through breaches, phishing or skimming, then run small transactions to validate the numbers before using them for larger fraud or selling the validated data on dark web markets.
Treat unusual clusters of small orders — especially from new accounts, mismatched geographies or repeated attempts on the same card range — as a likely card-testing signal rather than organic demand.
Use CVV checks so an attacker without physical card access has more difficulty completing a transaction, and AVS to check that the billing address matches the issuer's records.

Note the source's cost framing: each dollar lost to fraud costs store owners an average of about $4.61 once processing fees, lost inventory and operational disruption are counted (source-specific figure, not a benchmark to plan against).
Configure processor fraud analysis and automated rules rather than reviewing every order manually, because card testing runs at machine speed.
caveats: Financial figures are published estimates from the source and its cited research, not guarantees for any single store.
AVS/CVV alone do not stop all CNP fraud; enablers like tokenization and 3DS work with them.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Security_ Threats and Best Practices.docx

cards.title: Defend against digital skimming and payment-page tampering
cards.summary: Card skimming (Magecart-style attacks) injects code into checkout to steal card data; protect by minimizing third-party scripts and monitoring checkout code.
cards.use_when: Managing checkout page scripts, tags and third-party apps, or investigating an incident where card data may have been captured from your site.
steps: Inventory every script and app that loads on checkout and payment pages, including analytics, chat, A/B testing and tag managers, and remove anything that does not need to run at the payment step.

Restrict who can edit checkout templates and scripts, and require review for checkout code changes, since injected skimming code typically arrives through a compromised admin account or third-party dependency.
Use hosted payment fields or redirect flows so raw card numbers never enter your page's DOM where injected script could read them.
Monitor checkout code and script sources for unexpected changes, and route alerts to a named owner who can act quickly.
Include checkout integrity checks in your regular security review, alongside malware scans, so tampering is detected even if the script is served from a legitimate-looking domain.
If skimming is suspected, treat it as a card-data breach: isolate, rotate credentials, notify your payment provider and follow your incident process.
caveats: The source names Magecart as a category but provides no technical detection recipe; methods vary by platform and should be validated on systems you own.
No control fully eliminates skimming risk while third-party scripts run on checkout.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: Layer passwords, PINs and magic links for buyer authentication
cards.summary: Verify buyers with login credentials, card PINs, magic links or email verification so accounts and orders belong to real identities.
cards.use_when: Designing customer account login, guest checkout verification, or account-recovery flows for the store.
steps: Require authentication that proves identity for account access, using recognized methods such as client login credentials and card PINs at the point of verification.
For friction-averse buyers, use email-based magic links or one-time codes so verification does not require remembering a password.
Apply MFA or step-up verification to sensitive account actions: changing email or shipping address, viewing stored payment data, and issuing refunds or store credit.
Verify on the seller side too: publish enough business identity and contact information that buyers can confirm the store is genuine.
Align verification strength with the action: browsing can stay open, but saved-payment access and address changes should require re-verification.
Watch for account-takeover patterns in support channels, such as sudden email or address changes before an order, and add manual review triggers.
caveats: The source notes authentication solutions can require expert help if you cannot implement them yourself.
Stronger authentication adds checkout friction; the source does not provide a benchmark for how much friction is acceptable.
cards.source_name: E-Commerce Security_ Importance, Issues & Protection Measures.docx

cards.title: UI denial-of-service patterns that can lock down a storefront session
cards.summary: A malicious or compromised page can override ordinary browser escape routes — back button, close-window shortcuts, context menus — and a commerce operator should know these exist as scareware and annoyance vectors, not as legitimate merchandising behavior.
cards.use_when: Auditing suspect third-party scripts, promo takeovers, or scareware landing pages that trap shoppers, and deciding what to add to a monitoring or content-review checklist.
steps: Understand the mechanism set: intercepting keyboard events so Cmd/Ctrl-W does not close the tab (partly mitigated by triggering an alert/prompt between the Cmd and W keystrokes), pushing extra history entries so the back button cannot escape the page, spawning windows from every captured user event and refocusing them, hiding the cursor via a CSS property, and stacking dialogs on a timer.
Recognize the commerce-relevant abuse case: scareware pages that claim the device is infected and lock the visitor in to make a purchase pitch more convincing, especially to non-technical shoppers.

Defend by policy and process rather than by building the same tricks: restrict which third-party scripts run on your checkout and PDP, and screen any purchased traffic destinations for trapping behavior.
Note the modern mitigation: multi-process browsers can kill a tab stuck in an infinite loop without freezing the whole browser, and file-download prompts limit bulk silent downloads.
Do not use these techniques on your own storefront — the source frames them as attacks, and trapping visitors is a legal and trust risk, not a conversion tactic.
caveats: The source describes these as attack patterns demonstrated in a classroom setting; the card converts them into vulnerability recognition and prevention, not reproduction instructions.
Some mitigations described are historical and browser-specific; verify current behavior.

query: How do we prevent stored XSS in product reviews and customer-generated storefront content?

cards.title: Prevent storefront XSS with context-aware rendering
cards.summary: Keep customer-supplied content as data using safe rendering, appropriate encoding and sanitization.
cards.use_when: Handling any shopper- or admin-supplied content that gets displayed on your storefront — reviews, product Q&A, profile names, search terms, order notes, support messages, or header values.
steps: Trace untrusted product reviews, profile fields, search parameters and imported content to their rendering locations.
Use framework auto-escaping and safe text APIs for plain text; encode at output for the actual context.
Do not apply HTML entity encoding as a universal solution for JavaScript, CSS or URL contexts; avoid inserting untrusted data in executable contexts.
Where rich HTML is required, use a maintained sanitizer with a restricted policy.
Add a tested CSP as defense in depth and validate harmless stored/reflected cases on an owned test environment.
caveats: CSP and escaping are complementary; neither replaces authorization or secures every injection context alone.

cards.title: Use stored-injection defenses against self-propagating content worms in user-generated store content
cards.summary: Stored XSS that executes for every viewer can spread itself, so UGC surfaces need encoding plus containment.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing user-generated content surfaces on a store — reviews, Q&A, wishlist sharing, profile pages, social/community features, seller or marketplace listings.
steps: Recognize the worm pattern: the source's MySpace/Samy case shows injected code in a profile executing automatically for visitors and spreading without further attacker action — the storefront equivalent is content that runs for every shopper who views a page.
For any surface where one shopper's input is rendered to other shoppers, escape control characters at output so the input is text, not code.
Contain blast radius: limit the privileges of the context in which rendered content runs, and don't let UGC-bearing pages hold more session authority than needed.
Add moderation, allow-listed markup for rich content, and monitoring for sudden spikes in a page's outbound requests or injected patterns.
Test with a known-safe, owned staging environment rather than live customer data — the source's classroom demos are illustrative, not instructions to attack production.
caveats: Historical examples (MySpace worm) describe a platform and era whose mitigations differ from today's browsers and frameworks; treat the pattern as the lesson, not the exact mechanism.
Encoding prevents script execution but does not by itself stop spam, scams, or abusive content — those need separate moderation controls.

cards.title: Fix XSS with Context-Aware Output Encoding
cards.summary: Encode untrusted values separately for each output context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript string, URL) rather than escaping once at input.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or briefing developers on your storefront's product review fields, search results pages, or any template that echoes customer-supplied content.
steps: Identify every place customer-controlled data is echoed: product reviews, search query display, cart notes, custom engraving text, account names.

For each output location, apply the encoding matching that context: HTML-entity encoding in HTML body, attribute encoding inside attributes, JavaScript-string escaping inside script blocks, URL encoding inside hrefs.
Do not encode only at input or only once: a value written into a JavaScript string and then injected into HTML needs a second round of context-appropriate encoding.

Avoid deeply nested encoding chains where the same value passes through several languages or contexts; if a value must cross contexts, isolate it into a data attribute or JSON blob rather than embedding it inline.
Add a review step or linting rule so new template code that echoes user input gets a context check before release.
caveats: Encode at output, not just input; input filtering alone does not cover stored XSS in reviews or legacy data.
The source presenter calls deep nested encoding fragile and advises against it.

cards.title: Recognise reflected versus stored XSS and prioritise accordingly
cards.summary: Reflected XSS lives in the request, while stored XSS persists in your data and reaches every visitor regardless of the URL they use.
cards.use_when: Triageing vulnerability findings or designing storefront features: deciding where user data is stored (reviews, profiles, messages) versus only reflected in a response (search, filters).
steps: Classify a potential issue as reflected if the payload must be carried in a link the victim clicks (URL path or query).
Classify it as stored if the payload is persisted server-side — in a database, cache, or any durable field — and rendered for other visitors.
Treat stored issues as higher impact because the delivery route is irrelevant: the victim need not click anything from the attacker, so the whole user base is exposed.
Accept that the entry route for stored payloads can be obscure — an HTTP header, an API import, or a bribed insider — because any route to the data store suffices.
Prioritise fixes for stored flows: user profiles, uploaded content, review text, and anything that imports external data.
caveats: This is a classification framework, not a numeric severity scale; actual risk depends on the page and audience.
Stored XSS can be reached by means that would be impractical for reflected XSS, so do not use 'the attacker could not get them to click it' as a rejection reason.

cards.title: Treat XSS Filtering Browser Features as Unreliable
cards.summary: Built-in reflected-XSS filters can be bypassed and even aid attackers, so do not count on them as your storefront's XSS defense.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether browser-level XSS filtering removes the need for server-side sanitization on your storefront's reflected input pages.
steps: Assume the browser's reflected-XSS filter may decide not to block an attack, or may be absent entirely, and that some bypasses can degrade into new attack classes.
Keep reflected XSS prevention on the server and in templates: encode output by context and validate input, rather than relying on the browser to strip script from URLs.
When testing your own storefront, use your own staging copy, not third-party sites.
Verify the current state of any named browser filter before relying on descriptions of it, since browser behavior and availability change.
caveats: The source describes this as a historical browser feature; verify its current status before citing it.
No filter, header, or browser feature alone guarantees XSS protection.

Use when: Handling any shopper- or admin-supplied content that gets displayed on your storefront — reviews, product Q&A, profile names, search terms, order notes, support messages, or header values.

- Do not apply HTML entity encoding as a universal solution for JavaScript, CSS or URL contexts; avoid inserting untrusted data in executable contexts.

- Add a tested CSP as defense in depth and validate harmless stored/reflected cases on an owned test environment.
Caveat: CSP and escaping are complementary; neither replaces authorization or secures every injection context alone.

[0046b75dd21795789d7cfcbe] Use stored-injection defenses against self-propagating content worms in user-generated store content
Use when: Designing or reviewing user-generated content surfaces on a store — reviews, Q&A, wishlist sharing, profile pages, social/community features, seller or marketplace listings.
- Recognize the worm pattern: the source's MySpace/Samy case shows injected code in a profile executing automatically for visitors and spreading without further attacker action — the storefront equivalent is content that runs for every shopper who views a page.
- For any surface where one shopper's input is rendered to other shoppers, escape control characters at output so the input is text, not code.
- Contain blast radius: limit the privileges of the context in which rendered content runs, and don't let UGC-bearing pages hold more session authority than needed.
- Add moderation, allow-listed markup for rich content, and monitoring for sudden spikes in a page's outbound requests or injected patterns.
- Test with a known-safe, owned staging environment rather than live customer data — the source's classroom demos are illustrative, not instructions to attack production.
Caveat: Historical examples (MySpace worm) describe a platform and era whose mitigations differ from today's browsers and frameworks; treat the pattern as the lesson, not the exact mechanism.
Caveat: Encoding prevents script execution but does not by itself stop spam, scams, or abusive content — those need separate moderation controls.

Use when: Reviewing or briefing developers on your storefront's product review fields, search results pages, or any template that echoes customer-supplied content.

- For each output location, apply the encoding matching that context: HTML-entity encoding in HTML body, attribute encoding inside attributes, JavaScript-string escaping inside script blocks, URL encoding inside hrefs.

- Avoid deeply nested encoding chains where the same value passes through several languages or contexts; if a value must cross contexts, isolate it into a data attribute or JSON blob rather than embedding it inline.
- Add a review step or linting rule so new template code that echoes user input gets a context check before release.
Caveat: Encode at output, not just input; input filtering alone does not cover stored XSS in reviews or legacy data.

query: How should we secure store admin accounts with MFA, password storage and offboarding?

cards.title: Use unique admin credentials, MFA and compromise-driven password changes
cards.summary: Reduce store account takeover with unique credentials, stronger authentication and prompt revocation.
cards.use_when: You are writing the operating rules for who can log into your Shopify admin and how credentials are managed.
steps: Use long unique passwords managed in a password manager and enable strong MFA or passkeys where supported.
Block known-compromised passwords where the identity system supports it.
Change credentials when compromise is suspected or confirmed; do not adopt the source's arbitrary 60-90-day user-password rotation as a universal requirement.
Revoke access, sessions and tokens during offboarding rather than waiting for a password change.
Review login alerts and maintain a secure account-recovery process.
caveats: This updates the source's rotation advice using current NIST guidance; service credentials may need a separate lifecycle policy.
cards.source_name: How to Make Your Shopify Store More Secure.docx

cards.title: Staff Security Training, Least Access, and Offboarding
cards.summary: Lower insider and account risk by training employees, limiting sensitive-data access, enforcing password updates, and revoking system access on departure.
cards.use_when: Setting internal security policy for store staff, admin users, and departing employees.
steps: Ensure all employees are aware of the regulations that protect customer information.
Enforce password updates and require employee cybersecurity and privacy training to decrease liability.
Limit access to sensitive information so only staff who need customer data can reach it.
Revoke access to all systems when employees leave — the source frames this as preventing ex-employees from selling data to attackers or committing cybercrimes themselves.
Cover contractor and agency accounts that touch the admin panel, not just direct employees.
caveats: The source does not set specific password-update intervals or training frequencies; treat these as policy decisions to verify against your compliance obligations.
Offboarding is easy to overlook on hosted platforms where accounts proliferate — audit admin user lists periodically.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce security — what it means, common threats, and modern best practices.docx

cards.title: Step-up re-authentication for sensitive ecommerce actions (sudo mode)
cards.summary: Require the user to re-enter their password before a small set of high-impact account, payment, or address changes, as a defense-in-depth measure analogous to GitHub's sudo mode.
cards.use_when: Designing the admin/customer account flows where you allow changes to saved payment methods, shipping addresses, email/password, or payout/account details.
steps: Define a short, explicit list of 'sensitive actions' for your store: change password, change email, add/edit shipping address, add/remove a stored card, change payout/bank details, delete account, add an admin collaborator, generate API keys. Treat anything that redirects goods, money, or account recovery as sensitive.
Require the user to re-enter their password (or complete MFA) immediately before the sensitive action, then put the session into an elevated 'sudo' state.

Bound the elevation in time — expire the sudo state after a short window so a later request must re-enter. The source describes GitHub dropping the user back out after a while; set a window matching how long a real change takes, not hours.
Apply this on the server side per action, not just as a client-side modal, since the point is to require the secret even if an attacker already has session access.
Log every sensitive-action re-auth (who, when, from where) so you can review anomalies.

Note the secondary benefit documented in the source: this also protects against brief physical access to an unlocked device — someone who grabs a laptop cannot delete the account or change the payout bank without the password.
caveats: The source is explicit that this is 'not perfect' and does not cover every action — it is defense-in-depth, not a replacement for fixing XSS/CSRF or for MFA.
Adding re-auth adds friction; scope it narrowly to actions whose compromise is genuinely costly.

cards.title: Defense-in-Depth: Assume the Password Is Already Compromised
cards.summary: The source frames authentication design around building systems that stay secure even when an attacker holds the user's password, using layers rather than a single strong credential.
cards.use_when: Architecting login and account protection for a storefront where credentials commonly leak or get reused across sites.
steps: Adopt the source's working question — how can we build a system that stays secure when the attacker has the user's password? — as the frame for designing your login flow.
Layer controls: strong, length-based password policy, breach-list screening, rate limiting, a second factor, and monitoring for anomalous login behavior.

Because credential stuffing relies on reuse, verify login activity against indicators like new device/geography patterns rather than trusting the password alone (the source's broader security context emphasizes detecting failures rather than assuming none).
For sensitive actions (changing stored payment details, exporting customer data), require re-authentication or a fresh second factor even inside an active session.
Treat each layer as fallible on its own; the goal is that no single failure (e.g., a leaked password) becomes a full account compromise.
caveats: The source gives this as a design principle, not a specific product recommendation; pick concrete controls that match your stack and sensitivity.
No single control (password strength, MFA, CAPTCHA) is presented as sufficient alone.

cards.title: Store passwords with a maintained adaptive password hasher
cards.summary: Use purpose-built password hashing with unique salts and tested cost settings rather than raw fast hashes or reversible encryption.
cards.use_when: Reviewing how your store platform, custom app or admin panel stores customer and staff login credentials.
steps: Prefer the maintained identity system or framework password hasher over custom cryptography.
For new implementations evaluate current Argon2id guidance and platform support; retain a planned migration path for legacy bcrypt hashes.
Let the library manage salts and encoded parameters; a salted fast SHA hash is not a substitute for an adaptive password hasher.
Benchmark safe cost settings against login capacity, rate limits and current guidance.
Verify using the library API and rehash on successful login when the stored format needs upgrading.
caveats: Algorithm requirements can differ by platform or compliance context. Password hashing does not stop credential reuse, phishing or a compromised login endpoint.
